edges.description: Amplifier's modular architecture is inspired by the Linux kernel model.
edges.evidence: Amplifier is built on a modular architecture inspired by the Linux kernel model.

edges.description: In the Linux analogy, amplifier-core (Ring 0 kernel) provides mechanisms only, never policy.
Modules are Amplifier's analog of Linux loadable drivers and compete at the edges.
edges.evidence: Loadable drivers | Modules | Compete at edges

edges.description: The event bus and hooks are the analog of Linux signals/netlink, used to observe and control.
edges.evidence: Event bus / hooks | Observe and control

edges.description: Orchestrator modules are the analog of the Linux scheduler, letting execution strategies be swapped.
edges.evidence: Scheduler | Orchestrator modules | Swap execution strategies

edges.description: The context manager is the VM/memory analog and provides conversation memory.
The approval system mirrors Linux capabilities and is deny-by-default.
amplifier-app-cli is given as an example of the application layer.
The application layer is responsible for Mount Plan creation.
The application compiles a profile into a mount plan.
An AmplifierSession is constructed from a mount plan.
When a session receives a prompt it emits prompt:submit.
prompt:submit is an event emitted in the session execution flow.
After receiving a prompt, the session hands control to the orchestrator.
The orchestrator adds the user prompt to the context.
The execution flow calls the provider's complete method with the messages.
provider:request is emitted before calling the provider.
The flow processes tool calls returned in the provider response.
amplifier-core follows a Linux-inspired philosophy of providing mechanisms, not policy.
Anything two teams could want differently is policy and stays out of the kernel.
edges.evidence: If two teams could want different behavior, it's policy → keep it out of kernel.

edges.description: Loading modules is kernel mechanism; choosing which modules is policy.
Emitting events is kernel mechanism; deciding what to log is not.
edges.evidence: Emit events | Decide what to log

edges.description: The kernel provides hooks but does not select providers.
Managing sessions is kernel mechanism; scheduling execution is policy.
The kernel is intentionally minimal (~2,600 lines), changes rarely, and is meant to be small, stable, and boring.
edges.evidence: The kernel is intentionally minimal (~2,600 lines) and changes rarely.

edges.description: Kernel interfaces must stay backward compatible so modules do not break; evolution is additive only.
edges.evidence: Backward compatibility in kernel interfaces is sacred.

edges.description: New behavior comes from plugging in different modules rather than toggling flags.
edges.evidence: New behavior comes from plugging in different modules, not from toggleing flags.

edges.description: Module failures are isolated so the kernel stays up.
edges.evidence: Module failures are isolated. The kernel stays up.

edges.description: When a tool raises, the error is emitted as tool:error through the coordinator's hooks instead of crashing the kernel.
tool:error is an event used to report tool failures.
Adding a flag per use case is a red flag; flags accumulate, so modules should be used instead.
Passing the whole context for flexibility is an anti-pattern that violates minimal capability.
The north star is a kernel so small and stable that one person can maintain it.
edges.evidence: A kernel so small and stable it can be maintained by one person

edges.description: The north star includes a flourishing ecosystem of competing modules at the edges.
edges.evidence: A flourishing ecosystem of competing modules

edges.description: Improvements ship weekly at the edges while kernel updates stay rare and boring.
edges.evidence: Ship improvements weekly at edges, kernel updates are rare and boring

edges.description: Providers implement the Provider protocol.
The provider contract includes an async complete method taking a ChatRequest and returning a ChatResponse.
The provider contract includes parse_tool_calls returning a list of ToolCall.
Tools implement the Tool protocol with name, description, input_schema and execute.
The tool contract requires an input_schema property.
Orchestrators implement the Orchestrator protocol's execute method.
The orchestrator's execute receives a ContextManager.
The orchestrator's execute receives a HookRegistry.
Context managers implement the ContextManager protocol.
The context contract includes should_compact and compact methods.
A mount plan is the configuration contract telling the kernel which modules to load and how to configure them.
edges.evidence: A Mount Plan is the configuration contract that tells the kernel which modules to load and how to configure them.

edges.description: The mount plan is described as the configuration contract between apps and kernel.
edges.evidence: The configuration contract between apps and kernel

edges.description: Mount plans are the only way applications communicate configuration to the kernel.
edges.evidence: Mount Plans are the **only way** applications communicate configuration to the kernel.

edges.description: A mount plan must name the orchestrator to use.
edges.evidence: Which orchestrator and context manager to use (required)

edges.description: A mount plan must name the context manager to use.
edges.evidence: Which orchestrator and context manager to use (required)

edges.description: Providers, tools and hooks are optional entries in a mount plan.
edges.evidence: Which providers, tools, and hooks to load (optional)

edges.description: Tools are an optional entry in a mount plan.
edges.evidence: Which providers, tools, and hooks to load (optional)

edges.description: Mount plans carry agent definitions for sub-session delegation.
Agents are configuration overlays used for sub-session delegation.
edges.evidence: Agents are **configuration overlays** for sub-session delegation:

edges.description: An agent definition can override session settings such as the orchestrator.
An agent definition can override or limit providers.
An agent definition can override or limit tools.
Agents are not loaded at session start; they are used when the task tool spawns a sub-session.
edges.evidence: They're used when the task tool spawns a sub-session.

edges.description: The task tool is the tool that spawns sub-sessions.
edges.evidence: the task tool spawns a sub-session

edges.description: Creating a mount plan from a profile is described as the typical path.
The kernel validates mount plans before loading.
edges.evidence: The kernel validates Mount Plans before loading:

edges.description: Hooks register handlers for events.
Handlers are registered through coordinator.hooks.
tool:post is an event a hook can handle when a tool completes.
Hook handlers return a HookResult carrying an action.
A deny action blocks the operation.
An inject_context action adds to the conversation.
An ask_user action requests approval.
Every logged event record carries a session identifier.
Agents are specialized configurations invoked as sub-sessions for focused tasks.
edges.evidence: Agents are specialized configurations that can be invoked as sub-sessions for focused tasks.

edges.description: explorer is a built-in agent for breadth-first codebase exploration.
bug-hunter is a built-in agent for systematic debugging.
zen-architect is a built-in agent for system design with simplicity.
In interactive mode, an agent is invoked with the @ prefix.
edges.evidence: Use the `@` prefix to invoke an agent:

edges.description: An invoked agent inherits base settings from the current session.
edges.evidence: The agent inherits base settings from your current session

edges.description: Results of the agent's sub-session return to the main session.
edges.evidence: Results return to your main session

edges.description: Agents inherit the parent's provider and can override it.
An agent's tools replace the parent's tools when specified.
Agents inherit the parent's hooks and can add more.
An agent starts with fresh, isolated context rather than the parent's.
The same page says agents can keep context across invocations, which qualifies the fresh/isolated context rule (isolation from the parent, persistence across the agent's own turns).
edges.evidence: Agents can maintain context across multiple invocations:

edges.description: The current profile's agents section is first on the agent search path.
Installed collections are on the agent search path.
Best practice is to include only the tools an agent needs.
edges.evidence: Only include tools the agent needs

edges.description: An ended session persists its final state and is available for resumption.
Resuming a session loads history and restores context.
When a session ends its final state is persisted.
The CLI deletes sessions older than 30 days by default via session cleanup.
Conversation history is preserved when a session is resumed.
Collections are shareable bundles of profiles, agents, context files, and modules.
edges.evidence: Collections are shareable bundles of profiles, agents, context files, and modules.

edges.description: Collections can include custom modules.
edges.evidence: Collections are shareable bundles of profiles, agents, context files, and modules.

edges.description: Collections package and distribute Amplifier configurations.
edges.evidence: They provide a way to package and distribute Amplifier configurations.

edges.description: foundation is a built-in collection holding core philosophy and shared patterns.
developer-expertise is a built-in collection of development-focused profiles and agents.
The CLI installs collections from GitHub or local paths with collection add.
A profile can extend a resource from a collection.
Profiles are pre-configured capability sets that define which modules are available during a session.
edges.evidence: Profiles are pre-configured capability sets that define which modules (providers, tools, hooks) are available during a session.

edges.description: A profile determines what is available during a session.
foundation is the minimal built-in profile with just LLM access.
dev is the built-in full development suite profile.
base includes everything in foundation and adds tools.
base adds filesystem and bash tools.
The CLI can run a single command under a named profile.
Best practice is to extend parent profiles rather than duplicate them.
edges.evidence: **Use inheritance**: Don't duplicate - extend parent profiles

edges.description: Profiles should extend foundation or base and add only what is needed.
edges.evidence: Extend `foundation` or `base`, add only what you need

edges.description: Collections are the way profiles are shared.
Team profiles belong in .amplifier/profiles/.
The Anthropic provider is configured via the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable.
Ollama needs no environment variable because it runs locally.
Anthropic is one of the configurable providers.
~/.amplifier/settings.yaml configures the default provider and per-provider settings.
Multiple providers can be configured and the CLI switches between them.
edges.evidence: You can configure multiple providers and switch between them:

edges.description: A tool's execute returns a result with success and either output or error.
The authoritative tool contract specification lives in the amplifier-core repository.
Orchestrators control how agents execute: the loop structure, tool handling, and response generation.
edges.evidence: Orchestrators control how agents execute: the loop structure, tool handling, and response generation.

edges.description: The basic orchestrator is a simple request/response loop.
The streaming orchestrator streams tokens in real time.
The events orchestrator uses an event-driven architecture.
An orchestrator module's mount function mounts it on the coordinator.
The typical loop emits tool:pre before executing each tool.
The typical loop emits tool:post after executing each tool.
The typical loop emits provider:request before calling the provider.
Context managers handle conversation memory and state.
edges.evidence: Context managers handle conversation memory and state.

edges.description: Context managers implement compaction strategies.
Compaction strategy can be truncate or summarize.
Context managers support persistence.
A context module's mount function mounts it on the coordinator under 'context'.
The roadmap frames Amplifier as a Linux-kernel-like project with a small protected core and an experimental userland.
edges.evidence: Think of Amplifier like a Linux-kernel project

edges.description: The core is small and protected, something contributors should not need to touch.
edges.evidence: a small, protected core (which you shouldn't need to touch)

edges.description: Amplifier provides several orchestrators (basic, events, streaming) that control execution flow.
edges.evidence: Amplifier provides several orchestrators (basic, events, streaming) that control execution flow.

edges.description: The roadmap prefers leveraging emergent capabilities over building desired ones that don't yet exist.
edges.evidence: Focus is on leveraging emergent capabilities over seeking to provide desired capabilities that don't yet exist.

edges.description: A smart tool is standalone and is a library before anything else.
A smart tool is a library before it is anything else.
edges.evidence: It is a library before it is anything else

edges.description: Being a library lets the same capability appear in a CLI, a bespoke UI, an app, or any agent.
edges.evidence: same capability appear in a CLI, in a bespoke UI, embedded in someone's app, or driven by

edges.description: A smart tool must do something genuinely powered by a model.
edges.evidence: A smart tool has to do something genuinely powered by

edges.description: If every path is deterministic code it is a tool, not a smart tool.
edges.evidence: If every path through it is deterministic code, it is a tool, and that is fine

edges.description: Straight code paths still run with no AI provider configured.
edges.evidence: The straight code paths still run with no AI provider

edges.description: The caller of a smart tool is usually an agent.
edges.evidence: The caller is usually an agent.

edges.description: A failure names what went wrong and how to correct it so an agent caller can act.
edges.evidence: A failure names what went wrong and how to correct

edges.description: An MCP surface makes a tool reachable from MCP-only hosts but is not required.
edges.evidence: it makes the tool reachable from hosts that speak MCP and nothing

edges.description: Each new surface is an adapter over the same library and adds no capability of its own.
edges.evidence: Each new surface is a new adapter over the same library, and it adds no capability of its own.

edges.evidence: It must never be the only way,

edges.description: Deterministic code paths run with no model provider configured.
edges.evidence: the straight code paths run with no model provider configured.

edges.description: A tool must not refuse to load without model credentials; demanding a provider at load makes the AI capability mandatory.
edges.evidence: the tool must not refuse to load without them.

edges.description: Model-backed paths are ordinary capabilities of the library alongside deterministic ones.
edges.evidence: The model-backed paths are ordinary capabilities of the library.

edges.description: Deterministic capabilities live in the library alongside the model-backed ones.
edges.evidence: they live alongside the deterministic ones.

edges.description: Each distribution has exactly one manifest; a second SMART_TOOL.md is invalid.
A repository may ship several smart tools, each rooted at its own distribution.
edges.evidence: A repository may ship several smart tools, each rooted at its own distribution:

edges.evidence: structured data read from the copy built into the tool

edges.description: Callers reach the manifest through the library rather than locating a file, since install paths are not portable.

edges.description: The manifest body is prose for a reader, not an interface parsed by callers.
edges.evidence: The body is prose for a reader, not an interface.

edges.description: The manifest body feeds the rendered skill described in the invocation spec.

edges.description: A tool's skill body is the manifest body under a heading with the tool's name.

edges.description: The Agent Skills ceiling of 500 lines applies to the skill body.

Skill tiers follow Agent Skills' progressive disclosure: description, tool skill, capability skill.

edges.description: The manifest description is the first tier, deciding whether to look at the tool.
Capabilities compose by scripting against the libraries, where results are typed values, not text to parse.
edges.evidence: results are typed return values rather than text to

edges.evidence: a caller chaining capabilities reaches for the library

edges.description: State, caches, logs and temporary files belong outside the tool's own directory.
edges.evidence: State, caches, logs, and temporary files belong outside the tool's own directory.
